title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: B-Call methodology analyzing legislative voting data integrates two key dimensions: d1 (Ideological Position): Measures left-right political spectrum position legislator d2 (Political Cohesion): Measures consistently legislator votes ideological bloc Unlike traditional methods capture ideological position, B-Call provides richer understanding legislative behavior simultaneously measuring ideology voting discipline.

title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: rollcall data must data.frame : Legislators rows (rownames) Votes columns (column names) Values: 1 (Yes), -1 (), 0 (Abstention), NA (Absent) Example:
code: rollcall <- data.frame(   vote_1 = c(1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1),   vote_2 = c(1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1),   vote_3 = c(-1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1, 1),   vote_4 = c(1, 1, -1, -1, 1, 1, -1, -1),   vote_5 = c(1, -1, 1, 1, -1, -1, 1, -1),   row.names = paste0("Legislator_", LETTERS[1:8]) )  head(rollcall) #>              vote_1 vote_2 vote_3 vote_4 vote_5 #> Legislator_A      1      1     -1      1      1 #> Legislator_B     -1     -1      1      1     -1 #> Legislator_C      1      1     -1     -1      1 #> Legislator_D     -1     -1      1     -1      1 #> Legislator_E      1      1     -1      1     -1 #> Legislator_F     -1     -1      1      1     -1

title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: bcall(), also need clustering data: data.frame exactly one column named cluster Rownames matching rollcall data Exactly 2 unique values (can labels: “left”/“right”, “government”/“opposition”, etc.)
code: clustering <- data.frame(   cluster = c("left", "right", "left", "right",               "left", "right", "left", "right"),   row.names = paste0("Legislator_", LETTERS[1:8]) )  head(clustering) #>              cluster #> Legislator_A    left #> Legislator_B   right #> Legislator_C    left #> Legislator_D   right #> Legislator_E    left #> Legislator_F   right

title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: Let’s analyze sample rollcall data using automatic clustering: results contain: d1: Ideological position (higher values = closer pivot’s side) d2: Political cohesion (lower values = cohesive) auto_cluster: Automatically assigned cluster legislator: Legislator name
code: # Run automatic clustering analysis results_auto <- bcall_auto(   rollcall = rollcall,   distance_method = 1,  # 1 = Manhattan, 2 = Euclidean   pivot = "Legislator_B",  # Reference legislator; their side of d1 is positive   threshold = 0.1,      # Minimum 10% participation   verbose = FALSE )  # View results head(results_auto$results) #>                      d1      d2   legislator auto_cluster #> Legislator_A -0.9354143 0.00000 Legislator_A         left #> Legislator_B  0.5612486 0.83666 Legislator_B        right #> Legislator_C -0.5612486 0.83666 Legislator_C         left #> Legislator_D  0.5612486 0.83666 Legislator_D        right #> Legislator_E -0.5612486 0.83666 Legislator_E         left #> Legislator_F  0.5612486 0.83666 Legislator_F        right

title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: pivot reference legislator defines orientation d1 dimension: pivot’s cluster labeled “right” cluster becomes “left” don’t specify pivot bcall_auto(), cluster contains first row rollcall labelled “right” pivot taken . sign d1 arbitrary, function warns Important: pivot doesn’t change underlying analysis, interpretation. d1 values seem inverted, can either: Choose pivot opposite cluster, Simply interpret d1 values reversed signs

what: Real-World Example: Loading Data from CSV
title: Introduction to B-Call Analysis
text: ’s load analyze real legislative data:
code: library(readr) library(dplyr) library(tibble)  # Load rollcall data from CSV rollcall_data <- read_csv("votes.csv") %>%   rename(legislator = 1) %>%        # First column is legislator names   column_to_rownames("legislator")  # Option 1: Automatic clustering results <- bcall_auto(rollcall_data)  # Option 2: With party information clustering_data <- read_csv("legislators.csv") %>%   select(legislator, party) %>%   mutate(cluster = ifelse(party %in% c("PartyA", "PartyB"),                           "coalition", "opposition")) %>%   select(legislator, cluster) %>%   column_to_rownames("legislator")  results <- bcall(rollcall_data, clustering_data,                  pivot = "SomeSpecificLegislator")

title: B-Call Analysis for Legislative Voting Data
text: B-Call method analyzing legislative behavior integrates two dimensions: d1 (Ideological position): Places legislator left-right spectrum based average voting pattern. d2 (Cohesion): Measures consistent voting behavior . Low d2 indicates predictable voting; high d2 indicates volatility. B-Call? Traditional models like W-NOMINATE work well stable systems disciplined parties. fragmented contexts (like Chile Brazil), legislators low cohesion appear artificially “moderates” actually volatile. B-Call addresses explicitly measuring volatility second dimension.

title: B-Call Analysis for Legislative Voting Data
text: Provide rollcall data. package clusters legislators automatically Vote values (required format): - 1 = Yes/favor (voted favor) - -1 = /En contra (voted ) - 0 = Abstention/Abstención - NA = Absent/Ausente (vote) Understanding Pivot: pivot legislator crucial defines direction ideological axis (d1): - cluster containing pivot labeled “right” - cluster labeled “left” - d1 > 0: Legislators closer pivot’s cluster (ideologically similar) - d1 < 0: Legislators farther pivot’s cluster (ideologically opposite) choose pivot: - know data: Choose representative legislator political right → d1 > 0 represent right-wing positions - orientation appears inverted: Either change pivot someone opposite cluster, simply interpret d1 reversed signs - Without pivot, bcall_auto() labels “right” cluster contains first row rollcall picks pivot participation. sign d1 arbitrary, function warns
code: # Your data: data.frame with rownames rollcall <- data.frame(   Vote_01 = c(1, -1, 1, 0, NA),   # 1=Yes, -1=No, 0=Abstention, NA=Absent   Vote_02 = c(1, -1, 1, 1, 1),   Vote_03 = c(-1, 1, 1, 0, -1),   row.names = c("Leg_A", "Leg_B", "Leg_C", "Leg_D", "Leg_E") )  # Run analysis (automatic pivot selection) results <- bcall_auto(rollcall)  # Or specify pivot to control d1 orientation results <- bcall_auto(rollcall, pivot = "Leg_B")  # Visualize plot_bcall_analysis_interactive(results)

code: results <- bcall_auto(rollcall, pivot = "Leg_B")  # Access the main results data.frame results$results #                d1        d2 legislator auto_cluster # Leg_A -0.74352102 0.2785371      Leg_A         left # Leg_B  1.36481227 0.3977486      Leg_B        right # Leg_C -0.07685435 0.9476066      Leg_C         left # Leg_D -0.06203237 0.3582163      Leg_D         left # Leg_E -0.72360680 0.3908790      Leg_E         left  # Access metadata results$metadata # $principle: "PRINCIPLE 1: Auto-clustering" # $pivot: "Leg_B" # $threshold: 0.1 # $n_legislators_analyzed: 5 # ...  # Access R6 objects (advanced) results$bcall_object         # BCall R6 object results$clustering_object    # Clustering R6 object (bcall_auto only) # Get the data.frame df <- results$results  # Export to CSV write.csv(df, "bcall_results.csv", row.names = FALSE)  # Use in other analyses library(dplyr) df %>%   filter(d2 < 0.5) %>%  # High cohesion legislators   arrange(d1)            # Order by ideology

title: bcall 1.0.0
text: First CRAN submission. bcall_auto() warns picks pivot , sign d1 depends order rows. bcall() works single vote, metadata$n_legislators_original counts rows rollcall. Progress messages go message(), suppressMessages() silences , results short print() method. plot_bcall_analysis() longer uses deprecated aes_string(). dplyr longer dependency, plotly moved Suggests: plot_bcall_analysis_interactive() needs .
